title: The star formation region Gum 41
caption: The star formation region Gum 41, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla
celestial: Gum 41 · constellation Centaurus · about 7500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A red glow fills this view of Gum 41, a cloud of hydrogen and newborn stars. The Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on La Silla's 2.2-metre MPG/ESO telescope in Chile, took the picture.

The colour has a simple explanation. At the centre of this little-known nebula, brilliant hot young stars pour out energetic radiation. That radiation strips electrons from the surrounding hydrogen atoms, and when the atoms recapture them, they give off light at particular wavelengths, including the characteristic red of hydrogen.

That makes Gum 41 a textbook example of young stars lighting up the gas cloud in which they were born. The telescope recorded the scene through blue, visual and red filters plus one that isolates the glow of hydrogen, which highlights exactly this kind of energised gas. The official caption offers few further details about the region.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (29.78 x 29.82 arcminutes) and distance (7500 light years), the frame spans roughly 65 × 65 light-years. Its light set out about 7,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines B, V and R filters with a hydrogen-alpha filter. The caption says the red hue comes from glowing hydrogen, but the full filter-to-colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the red glow is much stronger here than it would appear by eye.
